replication.target_description: Prime letter-type effect: accuracy versus RT unresolved.

notes: Identity assessment: supplied candidate is an HTML transcription of the primary Brief Report, not the hosting site's AI summary. Article title, Emmanuel Ahr/Olivier Houdé/Grégoire Borst authorship, Journal of Experimental Child Psychology 145 (2016) 157–165, and school-aged negative-priming design match the supplied replication reference. The DOI itself is hidden as [Link] in this transcription, so DOI identity is not directly verified. Methods, Results, Discussion and References are reproduced with overlapping segments; no target PDF was supplied, so original PDF layout and the g2p glyph cannot be checked. Original paper is outside assigned scope; original and unassigned fields are placeholders only. The two assigned prime rows have identical descriptions covering BOTH accuracy and RT and the same p.5 locator (journal p.161); neither specifies which outcome it represents. Candidates: type-of-letters accuracy F(1, 75) = 10.75, p < .005, printed g2p = .13; type-of-letters RT F(1, 75) = 34.89, p < .001, printed g2p = . 32. No outcome assignment was made from audit ID or row order. Printed g2p identity is retained without interpreting its OCR glyph or converting metrics. Common-model participant candidate N = 78 is explicitly printed; final mutually exclusive grade counts 31 + 22 + 25 = 78 corroborate it. Recruitment was 95; children at chance (50% errors) on prime or probe were excluded. RT outlier trials more than 2 SD from individual condition means were removed (2.5%, 3.1%, 4.0% for grades 1, 3, 5); these are trial percentages, not participant N. Because row-specific outcome correspondence remains unresolved, N is a candidate in dispositions, not a positive row-level extraction. Authors explicitly describe probe negative priming as replicating adult effects, but do not give a separately mapped prime-outcome replication verdict.
